Munich massacre: 1972 Summer Olympics terrorist attack. The militants infiltrated the Olympic Village, killed two members of the Israeli Olympic team, and took nine other Israeli team members hostage.
Emerging in the 1970s among disillusioned liberal hawks, this political movement peaked in influence under George W. Bush and helped drive the push to invade Iraq in 2003 — what is it called?
Neoconservatism: Political movement of former liberals that combines political and social conservatism.
A Peronist who governed Argentina from 2003 to 2007, he later became the country's first 'first gentleman' when his wife succeeded him as president — who was he?

Néstor Kirchner: President of Argentina from 2003 to 2007. Néstor Carlos Kirchner Ostoić (25 February 1950 – 27 October 2010) was an Argentine lawyer and politician who served as the president of Argentina from 2003 to 2007.

One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Goguryeo and Silla, this kingdom in the southwest had the largest population of the three and was founded by Onjo near present-day Seoul. Which kingdom was it?
Paekche: Ancient Korean kingdom (18 BCE – 660 CE)
Considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, this painter and diplomat was known for dramatic, sensual compositions and designs for tapestry workshops — who is he?
Peter Paul Rubens: Flemish artist and diplomat (1577–1640)

Held every June in many cities to commemorate the 1969 Stonewall riots, this annual LGBTQ celebration of rights and self-acceptance began as marches in Chicago, New York, LA, and San Francisco in 1970 — what's it called?
Pride parade: LGBTQ celebration event. The events sometimes also serve as demonstrations for legal rights such as same-sex marriage.
This founding pharaoh of Egypt's 19th Dynasty had a brief reign that bridged the stable rule of his predecessor and the illustrious dynasty led by his son and grandson — who is he?
Ramesses I: Founding pharaoh of 19th dynasty of Egypt. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292–1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295–1294 BC.

Born in Southampton to parents of Indian descent who fled East Africa, this British politician served as Chancellor of the Exchequer before rising to the nation's highest office in 2022—but his tenure lasted just two years before losing to Keir Starmer. Who is he?
Rishi Sunak: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2022 to 2024.
Beginning on 24 February 2022, this conflict became the largest and deadliest war in Europe since World War II and sparked the continent's biggest refugee crisis in that span — what is it?
Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present): Phase since 2022 of war ongoing since 2014.
This Turkmen dictator gave himself the title 'Türkmenbaşy' — Leader of all Turkmen — and ruled the country from 1985 until his death in 2006. Who was he?
Saparmurat Niyazov: President of Turkmenistan from 1991 to 2006.
Lord of the desert and god of storms and chaos in ancient Egyptian religion, he murdered his own brother Osiris before being pursued for revenge by his nephew Horus — who is this god?
Set (deity): Egyptian god of the desert, storms, violence, and foreigners.
Nicknamed 'The White Death,' this Finnish marksman is credited with over 500 kills during the 1939-40 Winter War against the Soviets — who was he?

Born in Trinidad, this civil rights leader helped launch the Black Power movement while heading SNCC, then served as 'Honorary Prime Minister' of the Black Panther Party — and later took the name Kwame Ture. Who was he?

Emphasizing harmony with an enigmatic guiding force behind reality, this Chinese philosophical and religious tradition promotes effortless action, simplicity, and the three treasures of compassion, frugality, and humility — which tradition?
Taoism: Religious and philosophical tradition. Taoism or Daoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasizing harmony with the Tao 道.
Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu carved up China between 220 and 280 AD after the collapse of the Han dynasty — what is this era called?
Three Kingdoms: Period of Chinese history from 220 to 280 CE.
Leading Sweden's Moderate Party since 2017, this politician became prime minister in 2022 at the head of a minority coalition and went on to complete his country's accession to NATO. Who is he?
Ulf Kristersson: Prime Minister of Sweden since 2022. Kristersson became party leader after Anna Kinberg Batra resigned in 2017.
Once governor of Donetsk Oblast, this pro-Russian politician served as Ukraine's fourth president until the 2014 Revolution of Dignity drove him into exile in Russia — who is he?
Viktor Yanukovych: President of Ukraine from 2010 to 2014.
What is this — “2021 vehicular mass murder in Wisconsin”?
Waukesha Christmas parade attack: 2021 vehicular mass murder in Wisconsin. The parade was live-streamed, and other attendees captured the incident on videos later posted to social media.
Raging from 1914 to 1918 and nicknamed 'the Great War,' this conflict's mass troop movements helped spread the deadly Spanish flu pandemic — which war?
World War I: 1914–1918 global conflict. The war saw important developments in weaponry including tanks, aircraft, artillery, machine guns, and chemical weapons.

Rooted mostly among rural Indigenous communities in Chiapas, this Mexican far-left group has been in a frozen conflict with the state since 1994 and takes its name from a revolutionary agrarian commander — which group?
Zapatista Army of National Liberation: Far-left political and militant group in southern Mexico.
Who among these four was born earliest?
William Smith (geologist) (born 1769) is the earliest of the four. Financially ruined, Smith spent time in debtors' prison.
Who among these was born first?
Saint Valentine (born 175) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?

Stephen Gray (scientist) (born 1666) is the earliest of the four. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Which of these four came first?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four appeared first?
Lisp (programming language) (published 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Sally Ride is a physicist. Sally Kristen Ride (May 26, 1951–July 23, 2012) was an American astronaut and physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.

What is the atomic number of Neon?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
In what year was Jim Ratcliffe born?
Jim Ratcliffe: Sir James Arthur Ratcliffe (born 18 October 1952) is a British billionaire, chemical engineer, and businessman.
In what year was Thales of Miletus born?
Thales of Miletus: Thales of Miletus ( THAY-leez; Ancient Greek: Θαλῆς; c. 626/623 – c. 548/545 BC) was an Ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher from Miletus in Ionia, Asia Minor.
In what year was Ada Lovelace born?
Ada Lovelace: Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
In what year did Neil Armstrong die?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year did Wernher von Braun die?
Wernher von Braun: As a young man, von Braun worked in Nazi Germany's rocket development program.
In what year was Nitroglycerin discovered?
Nitroglycerin: It is combined with nitrocellulose to form double-based smokeless powder, used as a propellant in artillery and firearms since the 1880s.
In what year was Thallium discovered?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
Ceftriaxone: Pfizer. Ceftriaxone, sold under the brand name Rocephin, is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
In which country is Māori language?
Māori language: New Zealand. The southernmost member of the Austronesian language family, it is related to Cook Islands Māori, Tuamotuan, and Tahitian.
Who is credited with discovering Radium?
Radium: Marie Curie. Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
Who is credited with discovering Saccharin?
Saccharin: Constantin Fahlberg. Saccharin, also called saccharine, benzosulfimide, or E954, or used in saccharin sodium or saccharin calcium forms, is a non-nutritive artificial sweetener.
Who is credited with discovering Chlorine?
Chlorine: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this thinker is often called the "father of economics" and is best known for "The Theory of Moral Sentiments" and "The Wealth of Nations" — who is it?
Adam Smith was Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790).
Once thought to be the last living species in its genus after a related 'sea' cousin went extinct, this North American mustelid now thrives as an invasive species in Europe — which animal?
American mink (Neogale vison) is a semiaquatic species of mustelid native to North America, though human introduction has expanded its range to many parts of Europe, Asia, and South America.
A physician who called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress, this Russian writer produced four stage classics and ranks among modernism's founders — who is he?
Anton Chekhov was Russian dramatist and author (1860–1904).
Caused by poor circulation, lost nerve supply, or simple disuse, this process shrinks a cell, organ, or tissue below its normal mature size — what's it called?
Atrophy is the partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body.
Native to Southeast Asia, the glossy heart-shaped leaves of this evergreen vine are chewed together with areca nut — name the plant?
Betel (Piper betle) is a species of flowering plant in the pepper family Piperaceae, native to Southeast Asia.

Developed in Germany from the Old English Bulldog and the now-extinct Bullenbeisser, this medium-to-large mastiff-type dog breed is known for its square muzzle, underbite, and powerful bite — name the breed?
Boxer (dog breed) is a medium to large, short-haired dog breed of mastiff-type, developed in Germany.

One species in this genus of flowering shrubs, native to southern China and Indochina, has its leaves processed into the world's tea, while thousands of ornamental cultivars exist for the garden. Name the genus?
Camellia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Theaceae.
A secondarily aquatic clade within the order that also includes hippos, this infraorder covers whales, dolphins and porpoises, along with extinct relatives like Basilosaurus — which group of animals?

Cetacean are marine mammals belonging to the infraorder Cetacea, a secondarily aquatic clade under the order Artiodactyla that include whales, dolphins, porpoises and extinct groups such as Basilosaurus.
This tangor — a mandarin-orange cross — typically splits into seven to fourteen easy-to-peel segments — which fruit?
Clementine (Citrus clementina) is a tangor, a citrus fruit hybrid between a willowleaf mandarin orange (C. deliciosa) and a sweet orange (C. sinensis).
Made up of subregions called the genu, rostrum, trunk, and splenium, this thick nerve tract lets the brain's two hemispheres communicate — what is it?
Corpus callosum (Latin for "tough body"), also callosal commissure, is a wide, thick nerve tract, consisting of a flat bundle of commissural fibers, beneath the cerebral cortex in the brain.

Known by names ranging from the clinical to the crude to the childish — 'number two', 'dropping a deuce', 'doo-doo' — this basic biological process expels solid waste from the digestive tract. Name the process?

Defecation (or defaecation) follows digestion and is the necessary biological process by which organisms eliminate a solid, semisolid, or liquid waste material known as feces (or faeces) from the digestive tract via the anus or cloaca.
Best known for a single spiky, strong-smelling fruit beloved across Southeast Asia, this plant genus also includes eight other species with edible fruit — which genus?
Durio is a genus of plants in the family Malvaceae.
This inflammation of the small intestine is most often caused by contaminated food or drink, though NSAIDs, radiation, and autoimmune conditions can also trigger it. What is it?
Enteritis is inflammation of the small intestine. Duodenitis, jejunitis, and ileitis are subtypes of enteritis which are localised to a specific part of the small intestine.
Colloquially called 'squirting,' this phenomenon involves fluid from the Skene's gland and is physiologically distinct from coital incontinence — what is it?
Female ejaculation is characterized as an expulsion of fluid from the Skene's gland at the lower end of the urethra during or before an orgasm.
Often bonded to glucose to form table sugar, this white, water-soluble simple sugar occurs naturally in honey, tree and vine fruits, and most root vegetables — name this sugar?
Fructose is a common monosaccharide, i.e.

Designed at a major tech company in 2007 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson, this statically typed, compiled programming language borrows C-like syntax while adding garbage collection and built-in concurrency support — name the language?
Go (programming language) is a high-level, general-purpose programming language that is statically typed and compiled.
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, feeds only on blood, and has legs too short and stumpy to jump or even walk well on a flat surface — what is it?
Head louse (Pediculus humanus capitis) is an obligate ectoparasite of humans.
While first described from Virginia, this genus of flowering shrubs reaches its greatest diversity in East Asia, and some species climb up to 30 metres by scaling trees. What plant is it?
Hydrangea (or) is a genus of more than 70 species of flowering plants native to Asia and the Americas.
Resembling a lump of burnt charcoal growing on birch bark, this parasitic fungus is popularly called chaga — what's its scientific name?
Inonotus obliquus (a Latinization of the Russian word), is a fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.
A former Chicago financial options trader, this internet entrepreneur co-founded a nonprofit free encyclopedia as well as the for-profit wiki host Fandom — who is he?
Jimmy Wales (born August 8, 1966) is an American and British internet entrepreneur and former financial trader.
This American biologist and one-time Communist Party member had four husbands, the last being the physicist who led Los Alamos — who was she?
Kitty Oppenheimer (ne Puening; August 8, 1910 - October 27, 1972) was an American biologist, botanist, and a member of the Communist Party of America until leaving in the 1930s.
An indoor watchdog by tradition, this dog breed originated high in Tibet — which non-sporting breed is it?
Lhasa Apso is a non-sporting dog breed originating in Tibet.

This medical condition involves lymph nodes that become abnormal in size or consistency, with its inflammatory form sometimes distinguished as lymphadenitis and its infectious neck form historically called scrofula — what is it called?
Lymphadenopathy is a disease of the lymph nodes, in which they are abnormal in size or consistency.
In hermaphroditic species this reproductive pairing isn't strictly required, since self-fertilization is possible — what is the general term for it?
Mating refers to the pairing of either opposite-sex or hermaphroditic organisms for the purpose of sexual reproduction.
This Soviet tandem-seat helicopter was built purely for anti-armor attack missions, carrying no secondary transport capacity unlike the gunship it succeeded — what aircraft is it?
Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.

In this group of bone-marrow cancers, blood cells fail to mature properly and never develop into healthy cells, early on there are often no symptoms, though it can progress into acute leukemia. Name the condition?
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is one of a group of cancers in which blood cells in the bone marrow do not mature, and as a result, do not develop into healthy blood cells.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and the most common cause of gastroenteritis, this fecal–orally spread bug usually strikes about 24 hours after exposure. What is it?
Norovirus is the most common cause of gastroenteritis. Norovirus, also known as Norwalk virus, is the most common cause of gastroenteritis.
Part of the Bovidae family, this genus of seven social species is better known simply as sheep, all thought to trace back to the wild mouflon — which genus?
Ovis is a genus of mammals, part of the Caprinae subfamily of the ruminant family Bovidae.
Listed in the Dictionary of Fungi as containing over 300 species, this mold genus produces a compound that stops bacterial growth and also flavors certain cheeses — which genus?
Penicillium is a genus of ascomycetous fungi that is part of the mycobiome of many species and is of major importance in the natural environment, in food spoilage, and in food and drug production.
This scientific term for a group of fin-footed, mostly marine mammals includes walruses, sea lions, fur seals, and true earless seals — 34 living species in all. What is the term?
Pinniped are a widely distributed and diverse clade of carnivorous, fin-footed, semiaquatic, mostly marine mammals.
Lacking any real scientific definition, this British term for a large swimming crustacean has become almost interchangeable with 'shrimp' — what is it?
Prawn is a common name for small aquatic crustaceans with an exoskeleton and ten legs (members of the order of decapods), some of which are edible.

This small herbivore belongs to the family Leporidae alongside hares, and the European species of its genus has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica — what bouncy little prey animal is it?
Rabbit are small mammals in the family Leporidae (which also includes the hares), which is in the order Lagomorpha (which also includes pikas).

This English mathematical physicist shared a 1988 Wolf Prize with Stephen Hawking, won a 2020 Nobel for black-hole work, and dreamed up an 'impossible' triangle that inspired M. C. Escher — who is he?
Roger Penrose (born 8 August 1931) is an English mathematician, mathematical physicist, and philosopher of science.

Sitting near the center of the Milky Way between Libra and Sagittarius, this zodiac constellation's recognition predates Greek civilization, and it was among the 48 catalogued by Ptolemy in the second century — what's the constellation?
Scorpius is a zodiac constellation located in the Southern celestial hemisphere, where it sits near the center of the Milky Way, between Libra to the west and Sagittarius to the east.
This vertebrate organ system serves three main functions, protection, regulation, and sensation, and in mammals is made of multiple layers of ectodermal tissue. What is it?

Skin is the layer of usually soft, flexible outer tissue covering the body of a vertebrate animal, with three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation. The adjective cutaneous means "of the skin" (from Latin cutis 'skin').

Described as the most extreme form of malnutrition, this severe shortfall of caloric energy is so grave that deliberately inflicting it on a population is a crime under international law — what is it?
Starvation is a severe deficiency in caloric energy intake, below the level needed to maintain an organism's life.
Its Latin species name vulgare simply means 'common,' yet this Asteraceae-family perennial turned invasive after spreading from Europe and Asia to Australia and the Americas — which plant?
Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) is a perennial, herbaceous flowering plant in the genus Tanacetum in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
This viral brain infection, transmitted through the bite of infected parasitic arachnids, saw its European case count climb almost 400% over three decades. What is this arachnid-spread illness?
Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a viral infectious disease involving the central nervous system, transmitted by the bite of several species of infected ticks.

One of the two main forms of inflammatory bowel disease, this long-term condition inflames and ulcerates the colon and rectum, flaring up with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea before quieting down again — what is it?
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is one of the two types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with the other type being Crohn's disease.
The largest bird of prey on the Australian continent, distinguished by long broad wings, fully feathered legs, and an unmistakable wedge-shaped tail. What is it?
Wedge-tailed eagle (Aquila audax) is the largest bird of prey in the continent of Australia.
Discovered in 1849 and named for the Greek goddess of health, this nearly spherical body is the fourth-largest object in the main asteroid belt — which asteroid is it?
10 Hygiea: Fourth-largest asteroid. 10 Hygiea is a large asteroid in the outer region of the main asteroid belt, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

Nicknamed 'goutweed' and 'bishop's weed,' this shade-loving carrot-family plant is the type species of its genus and was introduced worldwide as an ornamental, becoming invasive — what is its scientific name?
Aegopodium podagraria: Species of flowering plant in the celery family.
With the general formula CnH2n+2 and every carbon-carbon bond single, methane is the simplest example of this class of hydrocarbons — what's it called?
Alkane: Type of saturated hydrocarbon compound.
First named by Karl Friedrich Burdach in 1822, this paired brain structure tucked in the temporal lobes drives fear, anxiety, and aggression as part of the limbic system. What is it?
Amygdala: Paired structure within the brain temporal lobe.
Who is this — “American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer (1971–2011)”?
Anwar al-Awlaki: American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer (1971–2011). Al-Awlaki was the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and assassinated by a U.S. government drone strike.

Also known by a folksy nickname, this small North American tree produces a custard-textured fruit tasting like banana or pineapple — despite containing a neurotoxin elsewhere in the plant. What species is it?
Asimina triloba: Species of tree. Asimina triloba, the American papaw, pawpaw, paw paw, or paw-paw, among many regional names, is a species of small deciduous tree.
This fig tree spreads outward indefinitely by growing extra trunks from its own prop roots, and its most famous species is the national tree of India — what is it?
Coined in 1814 by chemist William Hyde Wollaston, this polyatomic anion forms when carbonic acid loses a proton and plays a crucial role buffering the body's pH — what is it?
Bicarbonate: Polyatomic anion. It is a polyatomic anion with the chemical formula HCO−3.

A four-engined American heavy bomber from the 1930s, it dropped more tonnage than any other aircraft in World War II and ranks as the third-most produced bomber in history, after the B-24 and German Ju 88—what is this legendary aircraft?

Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress: American heavy bomber aircraft. The Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress is an American four-engined heavy bomber aircraft that was developed in the mid-1930s for the United States Army Air Corps (USAAC).
Also known as undulant fever or Malta fever, this disease is usually caught by drinking unpasteurized milk from infected animals and tends to persist for life — what is it?

Roughly a third of deaths from this group of over 100 diseases trace to tobacco, alcohol, obesity, poor diet and inactivity, and its malignant tumors are defined by uncontrolled cell growth that can spread — what is it?

Cancer: Group of diseases involving cell growth. Cancer is a group of diseases involving uncontrolled cell growth typically resulting in tumors with the potential to invade or spread to other parts of the body.

This branch of metabolism breaks down large molecules such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids into smaller units, releasing energy as cells convert the leftovers into waste like carbon dioxide and urea — what's it called?
Catabolism: Set of metabolic pathways that breaks down molecules into smaller units.
Built after a 1962 tech-transfer deal with the Soviets fell short on documentation, this Chinese fighter jet is a reverse-engineered derivative of the MiG-21 — which aircraft?
Chengdu J-7: Chinese version of the Soviet MiG-21.
Patented in 1967, this sympathomimetic drug helps people with asthma and other breathing disorders by acting as a bronchodilator — which substance?
Clenbuterol: Chemical compound which aids breathing.
Declared one of the world's most invasive species in 2000 and named Australia's top pest problem in 2008, which highly adaptable Asian bird thrives in cities?
Common myna: Bird of the family Sturnidae.
Nicknamed the jade plant or money plant, this low-maintenance South African succulent thrives on neglect and barely any water — what's its botanical name?
Crassula ovata: Species of succulent. It is sometimes referred to as the money tree; however, Pachira aquatica also has this nickname.
Designed to replace an earlier delta-wing jet for the French Air Force, this fourth-generation single-engine fighter first flew in March 1978 — which aircraft?
Dassault Mirage 2000: French jet fighter aircraft. Work on what would become the Mirage 2000 originated with the "Delta 1000" project launched in 1972.
In this heart condition, the heart chambers become enlarged and lose their ability to pump blood effectively, with causes ranging from genetics to alcohol and cocaine use — what is it called?
Dilated cardiomyopathy: Condition involving an enlarged, ineffective heart.

First imagined by Olaf Stapledon in his 1937 novel Star Maker and later named for a physicist who explored the idea in 1960, this hypothetical megastructure would encircle a star to harvest its energy — what is it?
Dyson sphere: Hypothetical megastructure around a star. A Dyson sphere is a hypothetical megastructure that encompasses a star and captures a large percentage of its power output.
The tallest and heaviest of all living penguins, this flightless Antarctic bird can top 45 kilograms and sports bright-yellow ear patches — which species is it?
Emperor penguin: Large flightless seabird endemic to Antarctica.
This Marine-turned-professor's 1981 memoir about fighting at Peleliu and Okinawa later inspired Ken Burns's The War and HBO's The Pacific, where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who is he?
This neurodegenerative prion disease has trouble sleeping as its hallmark symptom, most often stemming from a mutation in the PRNP gene — what is it?
Fatal insomnia: Prion disease of the human brain.
Sold under the brand name Luvox, this SSRI antidepressant treats OCD and other anxiety disorders, with milder side effects than most in its class except gastrointestinal ones — what drug is it?
Fluvoxamine: SSRI antidepressant. Fluvoxamine, sold under the brand name Luvox among others, is an antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class.
With a melting point of just under 30 degrees Celsius, this metal will turn to liquid in the palm of your hand — which element?
Gallium: Chemical element with atomic number 31 (Ga)

This Italian friar and cosmological theorist proposed that stars were distant suns with their own planets, and was tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for insisting the universe is infinite — who was he?
Giordano Bruno: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher and mathematician (1548–1600)
Unlike its rocky, mountain-dwelling marmot relatives, this solitary lowland rodent — also called the woodchuck — is common across the Eastern U.S., Canada, and Alaska. What is it?
Groundhog: Species of rodent. The groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots.

Often defined as the normal functioning of the body free of disease, pain, or injury, this multidimensional state of well-being can be promoted by exercise and sleep and harmed by smoking or stress — what's the one-word concept?
Health: Desirable level of functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being.
Also called urticaria, this skin condition brings red or flesh-colored raised, itchy bumps that may sting and often follow an allergic reaction — what is it?
Hives: Skin disease characterized by red, raised, and itchy bumps.
Defined as a blood level above 5.5 mmol/L, this elevated-potassium condition can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm and even cardiac arrest — what is it called?
Hyperkalemia: Excess potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels above 5.5 mmol/L defined as hyperkalemia.

ISO 56000:2020 defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — but the everyday version is the practical implementation of ideas, the cousin of invention focused on newness, improvement, and the spread of technologies. What's the word?
Innovation: Practical implementation of improvements. Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
Mentored by Louis Leakey, this English primatologist spent six decades at Gombe and revealed that chimpanzees use tools and form lasting social bonds — who was she?
Committed to accuracy and verification, this occupation and set of methods involves gathering and distributing the day's news — what field is it?
Journalism: Production of reports on current events.
Named from a Wiradjuri word imitating its own call, this Australian tree kingfisher's cackling laugh is a go-to sound effect for movie jungle scenes — what is it?
Kookaburra: Genus of birds (terrestrial tree kingfishers)
Also known as Peruvian ginseng, this Andean root crop is grown at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and exported worldwide as a dietary powder — what plant is it?
Lepidium meyenii: Plant species native to South America.
This American WWII twin-engine, twin-boom fighter carried its pilot alone in a central nacelle and served as fighter-bomber, night fighter, and long-range escort — which aircraft was it?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning: American twin-engined fighter of WWII. The Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Widely brewed as a calming herbal tea despite limited clinical evidence for its effects, this annual plant in the daisy family goes by the nickname 'scented mayweed' — which plant?
Matricaria chamomilla: Species of flowering plant.
Once made by roasting wood — hence its old name 'wood alcohol' — this simplest alcohol smells much like the drinkable kind but is far more poisonous. What is it?

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
Represented by symbols like '11' in the Hindu-Arabic system used worldwide, these mathematical objects serve to count, measure, and label — what are they called?
Number: Used to count, measure, and label. The most basic examples are the natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so forth.
Nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' this genetic disorder causes fragile bones and blue-tinted eye whites, usually stemming from faulty type I collagen — what is it?
Osteogenesis imperfecta: Group of genetic disorders resulting in fragile bones.

Also called the blue passionflower, this South American vine climbs via tendrils to 10 metres, bears fragrant blue-white blooms with a fringed coronal filament, and produces an edible but not particularly tasty orange fruit — which plant is it?
Passiflora caerulea: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
This Belgian-British microbiologist helped discover the Ebola virus in 1976, fought to contain its first recorded outbreak, then became a pioneering AIDS researcher — who is he?

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
